solution:
**a.** A **back cross** is a cross of the F1 hybrid with either of its two parents, the dominant parent or the recessive parent (for example Tt \(\times\) TT or Tt \(\times\) tt). A **test cross** is the cross of the F1 hybrid with the **homozygous recessive** parent only (Tt \(\times\) tt). So every test cross is one kind of back cross. But a back cross made with the homozygous dominant parent (Tt \(\times\) TT) is not a test cross, so a back cross is not necessarily a test cross.

**b.** The law of dominance says that in a dissimilar pair of factors one member completely dominates the other, so only the dominant trait appears in F1. This does not happen in every case. In **incomplete dominance** neither allele is completely dominant: a red-flowered (RR) *Mirabilis jalapa* crossed with a white-flowered (rr) plant gives pink (Rr) F1 flowers. In **co-dominance** both alleles express equally: red (RR) cattle crossed with white (WW) cattle give roan (RW) F1 with red and white hair. Hence the law of dominance is not universal.

**a. Dihybrid cross:** A cross between parents differing in two heritable traits, for example a cross between a round, yellow seeded pea plant (RRYY) and a wrinkled, green seeded plant (rryy).

**b. Homozygous:** An individual possessing identical alleles for a particular trait is homozygous (pure) for that trait. It breeds true and produces only one type of gamete, for example tall TT or dwarf tt.

**c. Heterozygous:** An individual possessing contrasting alleles for a particular trait is heterozygous (hybrid). It does not breed true and produces two types of gametes, for example the F1 hybrid Tt.

**d. Test cross:** The cross of the F1 hybrid (or any plant with the dominant phenotype) with the homozygous recessive parent, for example Tt \(\times\) tt. It is used to find out whether the individual is homozygous or heterozygous.

An **allosome** is a **sex chromosome**, a chromosome responsible for the determination of sex. In human beings and other mammals the allosomes are the **X and Y chromosomes**; the remaining 22 pairs of human chromosomes are autosomes.

**Crossing over** is the process that produces new combinations (recombinations) of genes by the exchange of corresponding segments between **non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes**. It occurs during **pachytene of prophase I of meiosis**, and its steps are synapsis, tetrad formation, crossing over and terminalization. It increases the chances of variation. The term was coined by Morgan.

**Phenylketonuria (PKU)** is an autosomal recessive disorder. Other examples given in the chapter are cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell anaemia and thalassemia. In PKU the homozygous recessive individual cannot produce the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase.

**X-linked genes** are genes located on the **non-homologous region of the X chromosome**; they have no corresponding alleles on the Y chromosome. A male has only one X chromosome, so a recessive X-linked gene is expressed in him, while a female needs two such recessive genes. Examples of X-linked traits are haemophilia and colour blindness.

**Holandric traits** are traits determined by **Y-linked genes**, which lie on the non-homologous region of the Y chromosome. They are inherited directly from father to son (male to male). Example: **hypertrichosis**, excessive development of hair on the pinna of the ear.

**Down's syndrome (21st trisomy)**. It is caused by non-disjunction (failure of separation) of autosome number 21 during gamete formation, so the individual has three copies of chromosome 21 and 47 chromosomes instead of 46.

**Haemophilia** (or red-green colour blindness) is an example of complete sex linkage. Its gene lies on the non-homologous region of the X chromosome, where crossing over does not occur, so it is inherited without separation. Hypertrichosis is a Y-linked example.

Mendel studied seven pairs of contrasting characters in the garden pea (*Pisum sativum*):

| Character | Dominant trait | Recessive trait |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Seed shape | Round | Wrinkled |
| 2. Seed colour | Yellow | Green |
| 3. Pod shape | Inflated | Constricted |
| 4. Pod colour | Green | Yellow |
| 5. Flower colour | Purple (violet) | White |
| 6. Flower position | Axial | Terminal |
| 7. Plant height | Tall | Short (dwarf) |

The law of segregation states that when the hybrid (F1) forms gametes, the two alleles segregate from each other and enter different gametes. The alleles do not blend or mix in the hybrid, so each gamete receives only one allele of the pair, either the dominant or the recessive, but never both. Each gamete is therefore **pure** for that character, which is why the law is also called the **law of purity of gametes**. This is shown by the reappearance of the recessive trait unchanged in F2 (for example dwarf tt plants from Tt \(\times\) Tt).

- When a single gene controls two or more different, unrelated traits, it is called a **pleiotropic gene**, and the phenomenon is **pleiotropy** (pleiotropism).
- Example: **sickle-cell anaemia**, caused by the gene \(\text{Hb}^{S}\); the normal gene \(\text{Hb}^{A}\) is dominant.
- Heterozygous **carriers** (\(\text{Hb}^{A}\text{Hb}^{S}\)) show mild anaemia, because their RBCs become sickle (half-moon) shaped only under abnormally low \(\text{O}_2\) concentration.
- Homozygotes \(\text{Hb}^{S}\text{Hb}^{S}\) die of total anaemia, so the gene is lethal in the homozygous condition.
- Thus one gene produces two different expressions: the sickle-cell trait in the carrier and lethal anaemia in the homozygote.
- A marriage between two carriers:

| Gametes | \(\text{Hb}^{A}\) | \(\text{Hb}^{S}\) |
|---|---|---|
| \(\text{Hb}^{A}\) | \(\text{Hb}^{A}\text{Hb}^{A}\) normal | \(\text{Hb}^{A}\text{Hb}^{S}\) carrier |
| \(\text{Hb}^{S}\) | \(\text{Hb}^{A}\text{Hb}^{S}\) carrier | \(\text{Hb}^{S}\text{Hb}^{S}\) sickle-cell anaemic (dies) |

- Normal, carrier and sickle-cell anaemic children are born in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1. The anaemics die, leaving carriers and normals in the ratio 2 : 1 instead of the expected 3 : 1. Carriers can be identified by microscopic examination of blood.

- His experiments were carefully planned and involved large samples.
- He carefully recorded the number of plants of each type and expressed his results as ratios, processing the data mathematically and statistically.
- He chose the pea plant, in which the contrasting characters are easily recognized.
- He studied the traits one at a time, or two or three in combination, so each result was easy to interpret.
- Each of the seven characters he studied was controlled by a single factor, and these factors assorted independently.

[Note: the textbook says the factors of the seven characters are located on separate chromosomes; not all of them are, but those sharing a chromosome lie far enough apart to assort independently.]

In humans, sex determination is of the **XX-XY type**. The male (44 autosomes + XY) is **heterogametic**: half of his sperms carry 22 autosomes + X and half carry 22 autosomes + Y. The female (44 autosomes + XX) is **homogametic**: all her eggs carry 22 autosomes + X.

| Gametes | Sperm 22 + X | Sperm 22 + Y |
|---|---|---|
| Egg 22 + X | 44 + XX (female) | 44 + XY (male) |

If an X-bearing sperm fertilizes the egg the child is a girl, and if a Y-bearing sperm fertilizes it the child is a boy, in a 1 : 1 ratio. Since the egg always carries X, the sex of the child depends on the type of sperm, so the father, not the mother, determines the sex of the child.

**Linkage** is the tendency of two or more genes present on the same chromosome to be inherited together; such genes are called linked genes. Linkage is **complete** when closely located genes do not separate (as on the X chromosome of *Drosophila* males), and **incomplete** when distantly located genes can be separated by crossing over (as for colour and shape of grain in *Zea mays*). It was discovered in plants by Bateson and Punnett and in animals by T. H. Morgan.

The number of linkage groups of a species equals its haploid number of chromosomes. The human haploid number is 23, so human beings have **23 linkage groups**.

- **Phenylketonuria (PKU)** is an inborn metabolic disorder caused by **recessive autosomal genes**.
- When the recessive genes are present in the homozygous condition, the enzyme **phenylalanine hydroxylase** is not produced.
- This enzyme converts the amino acid **phenylalanine into tyrosine**, so in its absence phenylalanine is not converted.
- Phenylalanine and its derivatives accumulate in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
- This affects the development of the brain and causes mental retardation.
- Excess phenylalanine is excreted in the urine, hence the name phenylketonuria.
- Being autosomal recessive, it appears in both sexes with equal frequency and tends to skip generations.

| Point | X chromosome | Y chromosome |
|---|---|---|
| Shape and size | Straight, rod like and longer | Shorter than X |
| Position of centromere | Submetacentric | Acrocentric |
| Chromatin | Large amount of euchromatin, small amount of heterochromatin | Small amount of euchromatin, large amount of heterochromatin |
| Genetic activity | More active | Genetically less active or inert |
| Non-homologous region | Longer, carries more genes (X-linked genes such as those for haemophilia and colour blindness) | Shorter, carries Y-linked (holandric) genes such as hypertrichosis |

Both have homologous regions with similar genes, and crossing over occurs only between these homologous regions.

[Note: the textbook says the X chromosome is metacentric; the human X chromosome is classed as submetacentric, its centromere a little away from the middle.]

Mendel published his work in 1866, but it remained unrecognised until 1900, when **Hugo de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak** independently rediscovered it. Advances in microscopy then allowed scientists to observe cell division and chromosomes. **Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri (1903)** studied the parallel behaviour of Mendel's factors (genes) and of chromosomes during meiosis, and on that basis put forth the **chromosomal theory of inheritance**, which identifies chromosomes as the carriers of genetic material.

The theory states:
1. Chromosomes are present in pairs in somatic cells, just as genes occur in pairs.
2. During gamete formation, homologous chromosomes pair, segregate and assort independently during meiosis, so each gamete contains only one chromosome of each pair, as each gamete carries only one allele.
3. The nuclei of gametes contain chromosomes that carry all the hereditary traits, so sperms and eggs are the link between parents and offspring.
4. Fusion of the haploid male gamete with the haploid female gamete restores the diploid number of chromosomes of the species.

**a.** The trait is **sex linked (X-linked recessive)**. A carrier mother and an affected father have a normal son, a carrier daughter and an affected daughter; an affected daughter appears only when she receives the recessive gene from both parents. The affected daughter married to a normal man passes the trait to her son, while her daughter is unaffected. The trait thus passes from mother to son through the X chromosome, the criss-cross pattern of X-linked inheritance, and is not equally distributed as an autosomal trait would be.

**b.** **Colour blindness** (red-green) or **haemophilia** shows this pattern of inheritance in human beings.

A **dihybrid cross** is a cross between parents differing in two heritable traits (two pairs of contrasting characters).

**Example:** a pure round, yellow seeded pea plant crossed with a pure wrinkled, green seeded plant. Round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r) and yellow (Y) over green (y).

1. **Parents:** Round, yellow (RRYY) \(\times\) wrinkled, green (rryy).
2. **Gametes:** RY and ry.
3. **F1:** all RrYy, round and yellow.
4. **Selfing of F1:** RrYy \(\times\) RrYy. Each F1 plant forms four kinds of gametes in equal number: RY, Ry, rY, ry.
5. **F2 by checker board (Punnett square):**

| Gametes | RY | Ry | rY | ry |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **RY** | RRYY | RRYy | RrYY | RrYy |
| **Ry** | RRYy | RRyy | RrYy | Rryy |
| **rY** | RrYY | RrYy | rrYY | rrYy |
| **ry** | RrYy | Rryy | rrYy | rryy |

6. **Result:** of the 16 combinations,

| Phenotype | Genotypes | Number |
|---|---|---|
| Round, yellow | 1 RRYY, 2 RRYy, 2 RrYY, 4 RrYy | 9 |
| Round, green | 1 RRyy, 2 Rryy | 3 |
| Wrinkled, yellow | 1 rrYY, 2 rrYy | 3 |
| Wrinkled, green | 1 rryy | 1 |

**Phenotypic ratio** 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, with four phenotypes. There are nine genotypes in the **genotypic ratio** 1 RRYY : 2 RRYy : 2 RrYY : 4 RrYy : 1 RRyy : 2 Rryy : 1 rrYY : 2 rrYy : 1 rryy. Round, green and wrinkled, yellow are new combinations, showing that the two pairs of characters behave independently of each other.

**Law of independent assortment:** "When a hybrid possessing two (or more) pairs of contrasting factors (alleles) forms gametes, the factors in each pair segregate independently of the other pair." It is based on the dihybrid cross: genes present on separate chromosomes separate independently during gamete formation and then unite randomly at fertilization.

**Example:** pure round, yellow seeded pea (RRYY) \(\times\) pure wrinkled, green seeded pea (rryy).

1. The gametes are RY and ry, and F1 is RrYy (round, yellow).
2. When F1 forms gametes, R and r separate independently of Y and y. R can go with Y or y, and r can go with Y or y, so four kinds of gametes form in equal proportion: RY, Ry, rY, ry.
3. Random fusion of these gametes in F2:

| Gametes | RY | Ry | rY | ry |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **RY** | RRYY | RRYy | RrYY | RrYy |
| **Ry** | RRYy | RRyy | RrYy | Rryy |
| **rY** | RrYY | RrYy | rrYY | rrYy |
| **ry** | RrYy | Rryy | rrYy | rryy |

4. F2 gives 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green.
5. Taking each pair alone, round : wrinkled = 12 : 4 = 3 : 1 and yellow : green = 12 : 4 = 3 : 1, the same as in a monohybrid cross. The 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio is therefore the two 3 : 1 ratios combining independently.
6. Two new combinations, round green and wrinkled yellow, appear that were present in neither parent. This shows that the factors for seed shape and seed colour are assorted independently.

**Test cross:** the cross of the F1 hybrid, or of any individual with the dominant phenotype whose genotype is unknown, with the **homozygous recessive** parent. It is a kind of back cross.

**Example:** a pea plant with violet (purple) flowers is crossed with a white-flowered plant (rr).

If the violet plant is homozygous (RR):

| Gametes | R | R |
|---|---|---|
| **r** | Rr violet | Rr violet |
| **r** | Rr violet | Rr violet |

All flowers are violet, so the unknown plant is homozygous dominant.

If the violet plant is heterozygous (Rr):

| Gametes | R | r |
|---|---|---|
| **r** | Rr violet | rr white |
| **r** | Rr violet | rr white |

Violet and white flowers appear in the ratio 1 : 1, so the unknown plant is heterozygous.

**Significance:**
1. It tells whether an individual with the dominant phenotype is homozygous (pure) or heterozygous (hybrid).
2. It is easy, simple, repeatable and predictable, since the recessive parent contributes only recessive alleles and the offspring show the unknown parent's gametes directly.
3. It is used to introduce useful recessive traits into the hybrids of self-pollinated plants during rapid crop improvement programmes.

**Parthenogenesis** is the development of an individual from an **unfertilized egg**, without fertilization. In honey bees, the drones (males) develop in this way.

**Haplo-diploid sex determination in the honey bee:**
1. The sex of an individual is decided by the number of sets of chromosomes it receives.
2. Females are **diploid** (2n = 32) and males are **haploid** (n = 16).
3. The female (queen) produces haploid eggs (n = 16) by **meiosis**; the male produces haploid sperms (n = 16) by **mitosis**.
4. A fertilized egg (egg n = 16 + sperm n = 16) develops into a diploid female (2n = 32).
5. An unfertilized egg (n = 16) develops by parthenogenesis into a haploid male (n = 16), the drone.
6. Diploid females become either queens or workers depending on their food: larvae fed on **royal jelly** develop into the queen (fertile female), and the others develop into workers (sterile females).

| Egg | Fertilized by sperm (n = 16) | Not fertilized |
|---|---|---|
| n = 16 | 2n = 32, female (queen or worker) | n = 16, male (drone) |

X-linked genes lie on the non-homologous region of the X chromosome and have no corresponding alleles on the Y chromosome. A **carrier** is a heterozygous individual whose one X chromosome carries the recessive gene while the dominant gene on the other X suppresses it, so she is physically normal but can pass the gene on. Only a female, with two X chromosomes, can be a carrier (for colour blindness, \(X^{C}X^{c}\)).

A male has only **one X chromosome**. If his X carries the recessive gene, there is no dominant allele on the Y to suppress it, so the trait is expressed. A male is therefore either normal (\(X^{C}Y\)) or affected (\(X^{c}Y\)), and never a carrier. Madhav's "carrier male" is an impossible genotype, which is why his marks were cut.

**Diagram:** the structure of a metaphase chromosome (Fig. 3.6). Labels: **chromonemata, centromere (primary constriction), matrix, chromomeres, telomere, secondary constriction (i) or nucleolar organizer, nucleolus, secondary constriction (ii), satellite**.

**Structure:**
1. Chromosomes are filamentous bodies in the eukaryotic nucleus, best seen at **metaphase**, when they are highly condensed. A metaphase chromosome is 0.1 to 33 \(\mu\text{m}\) long and 0.2 to 2 \(\mu\text{m}\) thick.
2. Chemically, it is made of DNA, histone and non-histone proteins.
3. A typical chromosome consists of **two chromatids** joined at the **centromere** (primary constriction).
4. The primary constriction has a disc-shaped plate, the **kinetochore**, to which spindle fibres attach during cell division.
5. A few chromosomes have one or two **secondary constrictions**. At secondary constriction I the nucleolus is organized during interphase (nucleolar organizer).
6. In very few chromosomes a **satellite (SAT) body** is attached at secondary constriction II.
7. Each chromatid contains a long, unbranched, slender, highly coiled DNA thread, the **chromonema**, running its whole length; a chromatid is one double-stranded DNA molecule from one end of the chromosome to the other.
8. The ends of the chromosome are the **telomeres**.
9. Depending on the position of the centromere, chromosomes are metacentric, submetacentric, acrocentric or telocentric.

Chromosomes mainly act as the carriers of heredity.

**Criss-cross inheritance** is the inheritance of an X-linked recessive gene from a father to his grandson through his daughter. Colour blindness and haemophilia show it.

**Example: colour blindness.** \(X^{C}\) is the dominant gene for normal vision and \(X^{c}\) the recessive gene for colour blindness.

**1. Colour blind male (\(X^{c}Y\)) \(\times\) normal female (\(X^{C}X^{C}\))**

| Gametes | \(X^{c}\) | Y |
|---|---|---|
| \(X^{C}\) | \(X^{C}X^{c}\) carrier daughter | \(X^{C}Y\) normal son |
| \(X^{C}\) | \(X^{C}X^{c}\) carrier daughter | \(X^{C}Y\) normal son |

All sons have normal vision; all daughters are carriers with normal vision.

**2. Carrier daughter (\(X^{C}X^{c}\)) \(\times\) normal male (\(X^{C}Y\))**

| Gametes | \(X^{C}\) | Y |
|---|---|---|
| \(X^{C}\) | \(X^{C}X^{C}\) normal female | \(X^{C}Y\) normal male |
| \(X^{c}\) | \(X^{C}X^{c}\) carrier female | \(X^{c}Y\) colour blind male |

The offspring are 25% normal females, 25% carrier females, 25% normal males and 25% colour blind males. The colour blindness of the grandfather thus reappears in his grandson, passed through his carrier daughter. The father never passes the X-linked gene to his son, because a son receives the Y chromosome from his father.

**A. According to the position of the centromere**, chromosomes are of four types (shapes):

| Type | Shape | Position of centromere |
|---|---|---|
| Metacentric | V shaped | In the middle, giving two equal arms |
| Submetacentric | L shaped | Slightly away from the middle, giving unequal arms |
| Acrocentric | j shaped | Near one end, giving one very short arm |
| Telocentric | i shaped | At one end |

**B. According to function**, the chromosomes of a cell are of two types:
1. **Autosomes**: chromosomes that control traits other than sex. A human somatic cell has 22 pairs of autosomes.
2. **Sex chromosomes (allosomes)**: chromosomes responsible for the determination of sex. Human beings and other mammals have X and Y chromosomes; the female is XX and the male XY. The X chromosome is longer and carries more genes, while the Y chromosome is mostly heterochromatin and genetically less active.

Homologous chromosomes are the morphologically, genetically and structurally identical pairs in a diploid cell, which synapse during meiosis.
